The '''Memphis Tigers men's basketball''' team represents the [[University of Memphis]] in [[NCAA Division I]] men's [[college basketball]]. The Tigers have competed in the [[American Athletic Conference]] since 2013. As of 2020, the Tigers had the 26th highest winning percentage in [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] history.<ref name="NCAA D1 Records">[http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/stats/m_basketball_RB/2011/D1.pdf NCAA D1 Record Book]</ref> While the Tigers have an on-campus arena, [[Elma Roane Fieldhouse]] (which is still the primary home for [[Memphis Tigers women's basketball|Tigers women's basketball]]), the team has played home games off campus since the mid-1960s. The Tigers moved to the [[Mid-South Coliseum]] at the Memphis Fairgrounds in 1966, and then to downtown Memphis at [[Memphis Pyramid|The Pyramid]], initially built for the team in 1991 and later home to the [[National Basketball Association|NBA's]] [[Memphis Grizzlies]]. In 2004, both teams moved to a new downtown venue, [[FedExForum]]. ''ESPN Stats and Information Department'' ranked Memphis as the 19th most successful basketball program from 1962 to 2012 in their annual ''50 in 50'' list.<ref name="go2">{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/blog/collegebasketballnation/post/_/id/62987/50-in-50-series-no-19-memphis|title=50 in 50 series: No. 19 Memphis – College Basketball Nation Blog – ESPN|date=August 23, 2012|publisher=[[ESPN]]|access-date=January 25, 2014}}</ref>

==History==
{{See also|List of Memphis Tigers men's basketball seasons}}

===Early years===
The predecessor of the University of Memphis, [[West Tennessee State Normal School]], first put a basketball team on the court in 1920. [[Zach Curlin]] began coaching the team in 1924. The Tigers joined the [[Mississippi Valley Conference (college)|Mississippi Valley Conference]] in 1928. The team played its early home games at a local high school gym, a local [[YMCA]], and in a room on campus called the "Normal Cage" which allowed only six inches from the court lines to the walls. In 1929, a $100,000 facility on campus named Memorial Gym became the Tigers' home.<ref name="history">[http://gotigersgo.cstv.com/sports/m-baskbl/archive/101899aaa.html Tiger Basketball History :: The early years<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

Curlin's last season coaching the Tigers was in 1948, by which time the school had been renamed [[Memphis State College]]; it would become [[Memphis State University]] in 1957. His successor was McCoy Tarry. In 1951, the new $700,000 [[Elma Roane Fieldhouse|Fieldhouse gym]] was opened for Tiger home games. In 1952, John Wallesea became the first Memphis State player to be drafted by the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]]. [[Forest Arnold]] became the school's first All-American in 1954. The Tigers made the [[NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|NCAA tournament]] for the first time, in [[1955 NCAA basketball tournament|1955]], under coach [[Eugene Lambert (coach)|Eugene Lambert]]. [[Bob Vanatta]] became the team's coach in 1956 and took the Tigers to the [[1956 National Invitation Tournament|NIT]] final. Win Wilfong became the team's second All-American in 1957.<ref name="history" />

In 1962, Dean Ehlers took over coaching duties. The Tigers began playing its home games at the [[Mid-South Coliseum]] in 1964. [[Moe Iba]] became the team's coach in 1966, the same year the team joined the [[Missouri Valley Conference]].<ref name="history" /> Iba's four years running the program are considered the low point in the history of Memphis basketball, with the team suffering 19 and 20 loss seasons before Iba's dismissal.  However, the Tigers did not remain down for long.

===1970s===
[[File:Mid-South Coliseum.jpg|thumb|right|200px|The [[Mid-South Coliseum]], home of the Tigers from 1966 to 1991.]]
In 1970, [[Gene Bartow]] was named head coach. The 1970 season also saw the first games of [[Larry Finch]] and [[Ronnie Robinson (basketball)|Ronnie Robinson]], two all-time greats. Larry Finch scored 24 points in his first appearance as a freshman. In 1971, the Tigers led by Finch and Robinson upset conference rival [[Louisville Cardinals men's basketball|Louisville]]. At 11–2, they were ranked #19 after not reaching the Top 20 in a decade. Early in the 1971–1972 season, Memphis State fell in a heart breaker to No. 2 Marquette after leading by five points with five minutes to go. After defeating Louisville in [[Freedom Hall]], the Tigers shared the Missouri Valley Conference title in 1972 with Louisville. Louisville won a playoff to represent the MVC in the NCAA Tournament while the Tigers went to the NIT for their fifth time.

During the 1972–1973 season, seniors Finch and Robinson led the Tigers to one of their most successful seasons. Memphis State won the MVC outright in 1972 after winning 14 straight games. They went to the [[1973 NCAA University Division basketball tournament|NCAA tournament]] where they handily beat South Carolina and Kansas State after a first round bye to reach the Final Four. After beating Providence, the Tigers went to play for the national championship against the [[1972–73 UCLA Bruins men's basketball team|UCLA Bruins]] led by legendary coach [[John Wooden]] and led by star [[Bill Walton]]. Keeping it close in the first half, the Tigers were overwhelmed in the second half eventually losing by 21, 87–66. Bartow won the NABC [[National Coach of the Year]] award that season and Larry Finch was named a consensus All-American. Also on the Finals team was [[Larry Kenon]] who went on to be a 2-time All-Star in the [[NBA]]. He remains one of the most successful NBA players in Memphis history. [[Wayne Yates]] took over for Bartow in 1974 when Bartow left for Illinois. Yates led Memphis State to three straight 20-win seasons, including an NCAA Tournament berth in 1976. The Tigers left the Missouri Valley Conference to become one of the inaugural members of the [[Metro Conference]] in 1976. [[Dana Kirk (basketball)|Dana Kirk]] became head coach in 1979.<ref name="history2">{{cite web|title=Tigers Basketball History II|publisher=University of Memphis|url=http://gotigersgo.cstv.com/sports/m-baskbl/archive/101899aab.html|access-date=March 12, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061028100723/http://gotigersgo.cstv.com/sports/m-baskbl/archive/101899aab.html|archive-date=October 28, 2006|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===1980s===
In the 1980s, the Tigers made seven NCAA tournaments and won three Metro Conference titles, amassing a record of 230–87 (.726). [[Keith Lee (basketball)|Keith Lee]] began playing for the Tigers in 1982, and Memphis was ranked number one in both major national polls for the first time the same year. However, that same night they were knocked off by [[Virginia Tech Hokies men's basketball|Virginia Tech]] 69–56 in [[Cassell Coliseum|Blacksburg]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anderson|first1=Mike|title=Tech stuns MSU|journal=[[Collegiate Times]]|date=January 11, 1983|page=A1}}</ref> In the [[1983 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1983 NCAA tournament]], the Tigers beat [[1982–83 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|Georgetown]] led by [[Patrick Ewing]], whom Lee dominated in the paint. They lost their next game to top-seed [[1982–83 Houston Cougars men's basketball team|Houston]] led by [[Hakeem Olajuwon]].<ref name="history2" />

After finishing 24–3 in the regular season, the 1984–1985 season proved to be another memorable one in Tiger history. Lee eventually led the team to another [[1985 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|NCAA tournament]] in 1985. Memphis State beat Penn, UAB, Boston College and Oklahoma to reach the school's second Final Four. They were defeated by eventual champion [[1984–85 Villanova Wildcats men's basketball team|Villanova]] and finished the season 31–4. All but one of the 12 players on this team were from the Memphis metro area.<ref name="cnn">{{cite news |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1122850/index.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212020715/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1122850/index.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 12, 2013|title=4. Memphis State – 11.26.84 – SI Vault|publisher=sportsillustrated.cnn.com|access-date=January 25, 2014 |date=November 26, 1984}}</ref> Lee was named a consensus All-American for the third time in his four-year career. In 1986, Kirk was forced out after becoming the subject of a criminal investigation. He was also found to have committed many NCAA violations as well. The Tigers were forced to sit out the [[1987 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1987 NCAA tournament]] and were stripped of all of their NCAA tournament appearances from 1982 to 1986, including the 1985 Final Four run. Kirk's top assistant, Larry Finch, one of the leaders of the fabled 1972–73 team, took over head coaching duties in 1986. One of Finch's first recruits, [[Elliot Perry]], began playing for the team in 1987. Perry led Memphis State to the [[1988 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1988]] and [[1989 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1989 NCAA Tournaments]] and was drafted to the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] where he became a successful player. In the 1988–89 season, the Tigers set a school record by starting the game against arch-rival [[Louisville Cardinals men's basketball|Louisville]] with a 24–0 run.<ref name="history2" />

===1990s===
[[File:PyramidArena.jpg|thumb|left|200px|The [[Memphis Pyramid|Pyramid Arena]], the Tigers' home from 1991 to 2004.]]
In 1990, Finch landed the country's highest rated high school recruit, [[Penny Hardaway|Anfernee "Penny" Hardaway]]. The Tigers also moved to the [[Great Midwest Conference]] and began playing their home games at the new [[Memphis Pyramid|Pyramid Arena]] (affectionately known as the "Tomb of Doom") in 1991. Stand-out Hardaway led Memphis State to the [[1992 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1992 NCAA tournament]], where the Tigers were defeated in the Elite Eight by rival [[1991–92 Cincinnati Bearcats men's basketball team|Cincinnati]]. The following summer, Hardaway was named All-American and earned a chance to train with the [[1992 United States men's Olympic basketball team|Dream Team]] before the [[1992 Summer Olympics|Barcelona Olympics]]. During the 1992–93 season, Hardaway earned Memphis State's first triple-double and then the first back-to-back triple-doubles in wins over [[Georgia State Panthers men's basketball|Georgia State]] and [[Vanderbilt Commodores men's basketball|Vanderbilt]]. On February 6, 1993, the school achieved its 1,000th all-time basketball victory in an upset over No. 4 Cincinnati. After the season, Penny Hardaway left for the NBA draft where he was selected third overall by the [[Golden State Warriors]]. He became the most successful NBA player in history to matriculate from the Memphis basketball program. In 1994, Memphis State changed its name to the '''University of Memphis'''.<ref name="history2" />

In 1995, the Memphis team included future NBA players David Vaughn, [[Cedric Henderson (basketball, born 1975)|Cedric Henderson]], and [[Lorenzen Wright]], and they made it to the [[1995 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1995 NCAA tournament]] where they lost in the Sweet Sixteen. Memphis joined [[Conference USA]] in 1995 as a founding member with long-time rivals Louisville and Cincinnati. Finch stepped down as head coach in 1997 and [[Tic Price]] took over thereafter. Price's three years were one of the Tigers' least successful since the 1960s.  He was forced to resign just days before the start of the 1999–2000 season after school officials discovered he was involved in an inappropriate relationship with a student at the university.<ref>{{cite web| url = http://www.nola.com/uno/index.ssf/2015/01/former_uno_mens_basketball_coa.html| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150114220657/http://www.nola.com/uno/index.ssf/2015/01/former_uno_mens_basketball_coa.html| archive-date = 2015-01-14| title = Former UNO men's basketball coach Tic Price finds love of coaching again at Lamar {{!}} NOLA.com}}</ref> [[Johnny Jones (basketball, born 1961)|Johnny Jones]] spent one year as interim head coach while the school looked for a replacement.<ref name="history2" />

===2000s===
[[File:Calipari CIMG0087.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Calipari directing his players during an away game against [[Conference USA]] rival [[Houston Cougars men's basketball|Houston]] in January 2007.]]
[[John Calipari]] was named Memphis' head coach in 2000. Under his leadership, the Tigers won the [[2002 National Invitation Tournament|2002]] [[National Invitation Tournament|NIT]] championship, then made the NCAA tournament in [[2003 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2003]] and [[2004 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2004]]. The Tigers left [[Memphis Pyramid|The Pyramid]] to play home games in the [[FedExForum]] in 2004. The 2005–06 Tigers were led by [[Darius Washington]], [[Shawne Williams]] and [[Rodney Carney]] and set a school record by going 30–3 and reaching a No. 3 ranking during a regular season that was capped by a [[Conference USA]] championship. In the [[2006 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2006 NCAA tournament]], the Tigers received a number one seed, and they advanced to the Elite Eight before falling to eventual tournament runner-up [[2005-06 UCLA Bruins men's basketball team|UCLA]].

Despite losing their top three scorers from the prior season to the NBA and graduation, the 2006–07 Tigers duplicated the previous year's regular season record of 30–3, were ranked as high as No. 5, and again won the [[Conference USA men's basketball tournament|Conference USA championship]], going undefeated in conference play. The Tigers earned a number two seed in the [[2007 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2007 NCAA tournament]]. The Tigers defeated 15 seed [[North Texas Mean Green men's basketball|North Texas]] in the first round, 7 seed [[Nevada Wolf Pack men's basketball|Nevada]] in the second round, and 3 seed [[2006–07 Texas A&M Aggies men's basketball team|Texas A&M]] in the Sweet Sixteen, and lost to 1 seed and eventual tournament runner-up [[Ohio State Buckeyes men's basketball|Ohio State]] in the Elite Eight.

[[File:Derrick-Rose-2008-Final-Four-UCLA.jpg|thumb|left|150px|Derrick Rose during the 2008 NCAA tournament]]
The [[2007–08 Memphis Tigers men's basketball team]] achieved a No. 1 ranking in the [[AP Poll|Associated Press basketball poll]] in January 2008, the school's first No. 1 ranking in the poll since 1982, and went on to win their third straight Conference USA title on March 15, 2008. After a month, they lost this ranking when they were defeated by in-state rival and No. 2-ranked [[Tennessee]] at home. Led by First-Team All-American [[Chris Douglas-Roberts]] and future No. 1 overall pick [[Derrick Rose]], the team received a No. 1 seed in the [[2008 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2008 NCAA tournament]] and defeated No. 16 seed [[UT Arlington Mavericks men's basketball|Texas-Arlington]] in round one, No. 8 seed [[Mississippi State Bulldogs men's basketball|Mississippi State]] in round two, and No. 5 seed [[2007–08 Michigan State Spartans men's basketball team|Michigan State]] in the [[NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Championship#Format|Sweet Sixteen]]. Memphis convincingly defeated No. 2 seed [[Texas Longhorns men's basketball|Texas]] in the Elite Eight round to advance to the school's first Final Four since 1985. Following this win, Memphis went on to beat No. 1 seed [[2007–08 UCLA Bruins men's basketball team|UCLA]] on April 5, 2008, advancing to the National Championship game on April 7, 2008. With this win, Memphis became the first team in NCAA history to achieve 38 wins in a single season.<ref name="msnbc_38wins">"[https://web.archive.org/web/20080405035409/http://beyondthearc.msnbc.msn.com/archive/2008/04/02/852777.aspx Could this year's champ be 'greatest ever']?" ''[[MSNBC]].'' April 2, 2008. Retrieved on April 5, 2008.</ref> After holding a nine-point lead with two minutes and 12 seconds left in regulation, the Tigers lost to [[2007–08 Kansas Jayhawks men's basketball team|Kansas]] in the National Championship in overtime by the final score of 75–68, becoming the second NCAA runner-up team in Memphis history.<ref>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore?gameId=284000063 "Kansas vs. Memphis Box Score"] ''[[ESPN]]'' April 7, 2008</ref>

The 2008–09 Tigers, led by another freshman guard, [[Tyreke Evans]], again went undefeated in Conference USA and earned a two seed in the 2009 NCAA tournament. The Tigers were defeated by the No. 3-seed [[2008–09 Missouri Tigers men's basketball team|Missouri Tigers]] in the Sweet Sixteen. Evans left after one year and was named NBA Rookie of the Year in 2010, the second straight Tiger to do so after Rose. On March 31, 2009, Calipari resigned to become the head coach at the [[Kentucky Wildcats men's basketball|University of Kentucky]]. In the months following Calipari's departure, nearly all of the incoming recruits who had committed to play basketball for the University of Memphis decommitted from Memphis and committed to Kentucky or other schools. The recruits included [[Xavier Henry]], [[DeMarcus Cousins]], Nolan Dennis, and Darnell Dodson.

On May 28, 2009, the NCAA formally accused the Tigers of allowing an ineligible player to participate in their games during the 2007–08 season.<ref name="commercialappeal">{{cite web |url=http://www.commercialappeal.com/news/2009/aug/20/memphis-tigers-found-guilty-ncaa-must-forfeit-2007/|title=Memphis Tigers found guilty by NCAA; must vacate 2007–08 basketball season, will appeal |publisher=commercialappeal.com |access-date=January 25, 2014}}</ref> On August 20, 2009, the NCAA Committee on Infractions announced that Memphis must vacate all 38 wins for that season as well as their appearance in the NCAA tournament and spend three years on probation. The NCAA alleged that Derrick Rose, a Chicago native, had obtained a fraudulent SAT score when another person took the test for him in Detroit, Michigan and his brother Reggie Rose was provided nearly $1,700 in free travel and lodging with the Memphis team.<ref name="go3">{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/news/story?id=4412279|title=Memphis also gets 3 years' probation|publisher=ESPN |access-date=March 29, 2021|date=August 20, 2009|first=Dana|last=O'Neill}}</ref>  The University of Memphis was not charged with knowingly fielding an ineligible player given that Rose had originally been cleared by the testing company and the NCAA. Rather, the NCAA imposed the penalty on a "strict liability" standard which held that Memphis must vacate their wins regardless of whether the school had any knowledge of wrongdoing by Rose and regardless of the NCAA's original clearance of Rose.<ref name="go4">{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/news/story?id=5018281|title=NCAA rejects Memphis' final appeal of vacated wins – ESPN|date=March 22, 2010|publisher=[[ESPN]]|access-date=January 25, 2014}}</ref>

===2010s – present===
On April 7, 2009, [[Josh Pastner]] was named the team's head coach. Pastner was hired as an assistant at Memphis in 2008 after serving as an assistant coach under [[Lute Olson]] at [[Arizona Wildcats men's basketball|Arizona]] for six years. Pastner gained a reputation as a strong recruiter during his tenure at [[Arizona Wildcats men's basketball|Arizona]].<ref>[http://www.cbssports.com/collegebasketball/story/11600010 Memphis promotes assistant Pastner to coach, replacing Calipari], by Gary Parrish, CBSSports.com, April 6, 2009</ref> In his first year as coach at Memphis, Pastner brought in [[Elliot Williams]], a transfer from Duke, who led the team in scoring and was drafted to the NBA. Williams was permitted to play his first season after departing Calipari took with him Memphis' top-ranked recruiting class.<ref name="scout">{{cite web|url=http://scouthoops.scout.com/a.z?s=75&p=9&c=14&cfg=bb&yr=2010|title=Scout.com: Men's Basketball Recruiting|publisher=scouthoops.scout.com|access-date=January 25, 2014}}</ref> In 2011 Pastner led the Tigers back to the NCAA tournament for the first time in his coaching career, though they lost in the first round to his former team, Arizona.

During the 2011–12 season, the Tigers announced they were leaving Conference USA to join the [[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East Conference]] starting in 2013 ([[2010–13 Big East Conference realignment|later renamed]] the [[American Athletic Conference]]).<ref>{{cite news|title=Memphis announces move to Big East|url=http://content.usatoday.com/communities/campusrivalry/post/2012/02/memphis-announces-move-to-big-east/1#.URsT7OjgL-Y|publisher=USA Today|date=February 8, 2012}}</ref> They began the season strong, moving as high to No. 13 in the country before falling out of the rankings (a phenomenon which would become a recurrent theme of the Pastner era). In the last game of the season, Josh Pastner's victory over [[2011–12 Tulsa Golden Hurricane men's basketball team|Tulsa]] gave him 72 career victories, the most by a Memphis head coach over his first three seasons.<ref name="commercialappeal2">{{cite web |url=http://www.commercialappeal.com/news/2012/mar/03/memphis-tigers-clinch-c-usa-title-78-66-win-tulsa/|title=Memphis Tigers clinch C-USA season title with 78–66 win in Tulsa |publisher=commercialappeal.com|access-date=January 25, 2014}}</ref> Memphis made its second straight NCAA Tournament after winning the Conference USA tournament. An 8-seed, the Tigers lost in the first round to 9-seeded [[2011–12 Saint Louis Billikens men's basketball team|Saint Louis]]. After the season, sophomore star [[Will Barton]] left for the NBA.

In 2012–13, the Tigers, led by CUSA player of the year [[Joe Jackson (basketball)|Joe Jackson]], won the Conference USA regular season and tournament titles in their last season in CUSA.<ref>{{cite web|title=Memphis Tigers clinch C-USA title|work=ESPN.com|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=330540235|date=February 2, 2013}}</ref> The Tigers began competition in the then newly formed [[American Athletic Conference]] in 2013. AAC competition was not as kind to the Pastner-led Tigers, as they earned an NCAA tournament berth in only 1 of the team's first 3 seasons in the AAC.

On April 8, 2016, facing mounting criticism in Memphis, Pastner took the job of head men's basketball coach at [[Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets men's basketball|Georgia Tech]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Smith |first=Jason |url=http://www.commercialappeal.com/sports/tigers/basketball/Source-Georgia-Tech-to-name-Pastner-head-coach-today-375027931.html |title=University of Memphis to pay Josh Pastner $1.255 million in settlement |publisher=Commercialappeal.com |date=2016-04-08 |accessdate=2021-11-20}}</ref>  A few days later, the Tigers hired [[Tubby Smith]] to take over the head coaching job.<ref>{{cite web|last=Smith |first=Jason |url=http://www.commercialappeal.com/sports/tigers/basketball/Tubby-Smith-agrees-to-become-Memphis-basketball-coach-source-says-375680321.html |title=Tubby Smith introduced as 'most accomplished coach' in Tigers history (w/ poll) |publisher=Commercialappeal.com |date=2016-04-14 |accessdate=2021-11-20}}</ref> Smith had just won the Big 12 coach of the year award as well as some national coaching awards for his season at [[Texas Tech Red Raiders basketball|Texas Tech]].

Smith was fired on March 14, 2018, after failing to reach the NCAA Tournament in both of his two years as head coach. [[Penny Hardaway]] was later confirmed as Smith's replacement.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cbssports.com/college-basketball/news/memphis-reaches-agreement-with-penny-hardaway-to-become-next-head-coach/|title=Memphis reaches agreement with Penny Hardaway to become next head coach|work=CBSSports.com|access-date=March 20, 2018|language=en}}</ref>

On March 28, 2021, the Tigers won their second NIT tournament with a 77–65 win over the #4 seed Mississippi State Bulldogs, finishing their season at 20–8.<ref>{{cite web|title=Memphis Wins 2021 NIT Championship|publisher=ncaa.com|url=https://www.ncaa.com/news/basketball-men/article/2021-03-28/memphis-defeats-mississippi-state-win-2021-nit-championship|date=March 28, 2021}}</ref>

On June 11, 2021 speculation began to circulate that Penny Hardaway was a candidate for multiple head coaching jobs in the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]], including his former team the [[Orlando Magic]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Cordner|first=Jason|date=2021-06-11|title=Penny Hardaway Draws Interest of Several NBA Teams For Head Coach|url=https://thesource.com/2021/06/11/source-sports-penny-hardaway-draws-interest-of-several-nba-teams-for-head-coach/|access-date=2021-06-30|website=The Source|language=en-US}}</ref> On June 28, reports emerged that Hardaway had in fact interviewed and emerged as a top candidate for the Magic's vacant head coaching job.<ref>{{cite web|last=Cali|first=Mike|date=2021-06-27|title=Report: Penny Hardaway interviewed for Orlando Magic head coaching job and is a "serious candidate"|url=https://www.orlandopinstripedpost.com/2021/6/27/22553215/orlando-magic-penny-hardaway-interview-nba-head-coach|access-date=2021-06-30|website=Orlando Pinstriped Post|language=en}}</ref> Two days later, via Instagram, Hardaway confirmed he was not leaving the University of Memphis, and reports emerged the same day that [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame|Hall of Fame]] coach [[Larry Brown (basketball)|Larry Brown]] had accepted an offer to be his assistant.<ref>{{cite web|title=Penny Hardaway won't coach Magic, reportedly hires Hall of Famer Larry Brown as Memphis assistant|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/penny-hardaway-wont-coach-magic-reportedly-hires-larry-brown-as-memphis-assistant-034954110.html|access-date=2021-06-30|website=sports.yahoo.com|language=en-US}}</ref>  Brown was an assistant coach for the 2021-22 season, but changed his role to advisor for the 2022-23 season, and left the program for health reasons in December 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-09 |title=Brown steps down at Memphis due to health |url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/story/_/id/35219779/larry-brown-steps-memphis-due-health-concerns |access-date=2024-09-06 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref>

=== Basketball Hall of Fame ===
The Memphis program has had two coaches inducted into the [[National Collegiate Basketball Hall of Fame|National College Basketball Hall of Fame]] ([[Gene Bartow]]) and [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame]] ([[John Calipari]]). The school has yet to produce any players that have been inducted. Larry Brown was hired as an assistant in 2021 and was already a member of both the College and Naismith halls of fame.

==Memphis Tigers in the NBA==
{{Main|List of Memphis Tigers in the NBA}}
Since the [[NBA draft]] began in 1947, 52 players from Memphis have been drafted, with an additional nine played after being signed as undrafted free agents. Of the 52 drafted players, 28 played in at least one NBA (or ABA) game. Memphis has produced 14 first-round picks, including 8 top-ten picks and one number-one pick ([[Derrick Rose]]). Three former Tigers have been named [[NBA All-Star Game|NBA All-Stars]]: [[Larry Kenon]] (twice), [[Penny Hardaway]] (4 times), and Derrick Rose (3 times). Four have gone on to win the NBA Championship: [[Win Wilfong]] with the [[St. Louis Hawks]] in [[1957–58 NBA season|1958]], [[William Bedford (basketball)|William Bedford]] with the [[Detroit Pistons]] in [[1989–90 NBA season|1990]], [[Earl Barron]] with the [[Miami Heat]] in [[2005–06 NBA season|2006]], and [[James Wiseman]] with the [[Golden State Warriors]] in [[2021–22 NBA season|2022]]. In 2010, Memphis became the second college to produce two consecutive [[NBA Rookie of the Year]] winners: Derrick Rose in 2009 and [[Tyreke Evans]] in 2010 (the first being [[North Carolina Tar Heels men's basketball|North Carolina]] with winners [[Walter Davis (basketball)|Walter Davis]] in [[1977–78 NBA season|1978]] and [[Phil Ford (basketball)|Phil Ford]] in [[1978–79 NBA season|1979]]). In 2011, Rose became the first former Tiger to be named the [[NBA Most Valuable Player]]. Many Memphis players since the 1960s that have gone undrafted or had unsuccessful NBA careers have also played in professional leagues in Europe, Asia and/or Latin America.
